# Sandglass master list

Generated from the game code by `npm run master-list`. Do not edit by hand: change the element data in `src/sim/elements.ts` (or the rules in `src/sim/chem.ts`) and run the script again.

231 elements. Every pair of elements is listed below, in both directions, with what happens and why.

## World rules

- Room temperature is 20 °C. Empty cells are air; air slowly drifts back to room temperature, which is how hot things cool and steam condenses.
- Air feeds fire with oxygen strength 0.21. Burning turns touching air into smoke, which feeds nothing, so a sealed space runs out of air.
- The bottom and side edges are walls. Gases that vent (smoke) leave through the top edge, and smoke fades to a faint haze as it ages; others stay.
- Gravity is per element: each falling element has its own acceleration and top speed.
- Heat flows between touching cells by conduction (each element has a conductivity and heat capacity). Burning cells also push radiant heat into their neighbours.
- Movement only swaps cells, so nothing is created or lost by moving. Reactions and burning change cells into other elements.

## Rule families

The chemistry compiler applies these general rules to every pair of elements; nobody writes pairs by hand. Hand-written overrides, if any, win.

| Rule | Happens when | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Density | A heavier powder or liquid touches a lighter liquid or gas | It sinks through, swapping places; the bigger the gap, the faster |
| Melting, boiling | A cell gets hotter than its melting or boiling point | It becomes its melted or boiled form and absorbs a little heat |
| Freezing, condensing | A cell gets colder than the point of whatever melts or boils into it | It becomes that element and releases a little heat |
| Rubble | A solid would form (freeze) with nothing solid under it | It forms as its loose rubble instead (lava → gravel) |
| Combustion | A flammable cell is at its ignition point and touches an oxidiser, or a loose flame touches it | It becomes fire that remembers its fuel, burns for its fuel time, then leaves its residue |
| Corrosion | An acid touches metal, rock or wood softer than its acidity | Both cells are used up; metal gives off hydrogen |
| Neutralisation | An acid touches a base | Both become water and warm up; a carbonate base fizzes into carbon dioxide |
| Quenching | Water touches a flame or a burning cell | The fire goes out; the water may flash into steam |
| Setting | Water touches a powder that sets (cement, quicklime) | The powder takes in the water and hardens, sometimes getting hot |
| Thawing | Salt or sugar touches ice | The ice melts into water |
| Acid gas | Sulfur dioxide or chlorine touches water | The water turns into acid |
| Toxic gas | A toxic gas touches a living thing | It withers |
| Rusting | Water or oxygen touches a metal that rusts | It slowly turns into rust |
| Rotting | Water touches dead organic matter | It slowly rots into dirt |
| Baking | A cell passes its baking point | A one-way change (clay to brick), sometimes giving off a gas |

## Elements

### Wall

An indestructible solid. Never moves. Nothing melts, burns or eats it; use it for containers and floors.

- **State:** Solid, 2,500 kg/m³
- **Hardness:** 1 (acid stronger than this eats it)

### Sand

A fine, heavy powder. Falls, piles into slopes and sinks through lighter liquids. Very hard to melt or eat away.

- **State:** Powder, 1,600 kg/m³
- **In liquids:** Sinks through liquids lighter than 1,600 kg/m³, rests on heavier ones
- **Falls:** up to 165 cells/s
- **Bakes:** at 1,450 °C into molten glass; there is no way back
- **Soaks up:** water, up to 30% of a cell; wet, it holds steeper slopes and will not burn
- **Hardness:** 0.95 (acid stronger than this eats it)

With other elements (63 interact):

- **Water:** Sand soaks up water: it is porous and holds up to 30% water. Sand sinks through water (1,600 vs 1,000 kg/m³).
- **Oil:** Sand sinks through oil (1,600 vs 900 kg/m³).
- **Steam:** Sand falls through steam.
- **Fire:** Sand falls through fire.
- **Smoke:** Sand falls through smoke.
- **Acid:** Sand sinks through acid (1,600 vs 1,100 kg/m³).
- **Hydrogen:** Sand falls through hydrogen.
- **Oxygen:** Sand falls through oxygen.
- **Methane:** Sand falls through methane.

### Water

A runny liquid. Flows and settles flat. Boils into steam when hot, freezes into ice when cold, and cools what it touches.

- **State:** Liquid, 1,000 kg/m³
- **In liquids:** Sinks through liquids lighter than 1,000 kg/m³, floats on heavier ones
- **Falls:** up to 165 cells/s
- **Boils:** at 100 °C, into steam
- **Freezes:** below 0 °C, into ice
- **Conducts:** only when it carries salt; current then splits it into hydrogen and oxygen
- **Absorbs:** neutrons, slowing a chain reaction nearby
- **Dissolves:** soluble powders (salt, sugar), up to each one’s limit; saltier is heavier

### Wood

A solid fuel. Stays put. Catches fire where it touches air once hot enough, and burns down to a little ash.

- **State:** Solid, 700 kg/m³
- **Burns:** from 300 °C in air, 2.5 s per cell, leaves ash

### Battery

A power cell. Stays put. Painted into a loop of wire, it drives current round the loop, whichever way it fits; with no closed loop, nothing flows. Each cell along the wire adds 1.5 volts, and a thicker battery gives more current. It runs flat with use, and a long short circuit can make it burst into flame.

- **State:** Solid, 2,500 kg/m³
- **Burns:** from 200 °C in air, 2.67 s per cell, leaves ash
- **Powers:** 1.5 V for each cell along the wire, round a closed loop; turns itself round to help other batteries; runs flat with use
- **Hardness:** 0.6 (acid stronger than this eats it)

### Flour

### Propane

A fuel gas, heavier than air. Sinks and pools in low places. Its vapour catches from any flame and burns hot into steam.

- **State:** Gas, 1.88 kg/m³
- **In air:** Sinks slowly (heavier than air)

### Dry ice

Frozen carbon dioxide, very cold. Stays put and turns straight into gas without melting, chilling everything nearby.

- **State:** Solid, 1,560 kg/m³
- **Starts at:** -79 °C
- **Sublimes:** at -78 °C, into carbon dioxide
- **Span:** reaches 4 cells past its support; beyond that, or with nothing under it, it breaks off and falls

### Bulb

- **Conducts:** current, resisting it (3 Ω a cell) and heating as it passes
- **Glows:** as hot as the power through it allows: brighter with more current
- **Glows:** when current heats it, fading when the power stops

- **Opens:** above 60 °C and closes again below 45 °C

- **State:** Solid, 2,000 kg/m³
- **Burns:** from 900 °C in air, 3.33 s per cell, leaves ash
- **Conducts:** current, resisting it (100 Ω a cell) and heating as it passes
- **Hardness:** 0.7 (acid stronger than this eats it)

### Electromagnet

Copper wire coiled round an iron core. Stays put. While current runs through it, it pulls iron filings like a magnet, harder the more current; cut the power and it lets them go.

- **State:** Solid, 7,800 kg/m³
- **Conducts:** current, resisting it (1 Ω a cell) and heating as it passes
- **Pulls:** iron filings within 14 cells while current runs through it
- **Bakes:** at 1,085 °C into molten copper; there is no way back
- **Hardness:** 0.7 (acid stronger than this eats it)

With other elements (1 interact):

- **Acid:** Acid eats electromagnet: acidity 0.8 beats hardness 0.7, giving off hydrogen.

### Graphite

Soft grey carbon, a powder. Falls and piles, and carries current where its grains touch, with some resistance, so a pile warms under load. In great heat it burns slowly into carbon dioxide.

- **State:** Powder, 2,200 kg/m³
- **In liquids:** Sinks through liquids lighter than 2,200 kg/m³, rests on heavier ones
- **Burns:** from 750 °C in air, 6.67 s per cell, leaves carbon dioxide
- **Conducts:** current with almost no resistance
- **A flame:** will not light it; it needs 750 °C
- **Hardness:** 0.3 (acid stronger than this eats it)

### Molten iron

Melted iron, white-hot and heavy. Flows and sinks through water and rock. Sets back into iron as it cools.

- **State:** Liquid, 6,980 kg/m³
- **Starts at:** 1,600 °C
- **In liquids:** Sinks through liquids lighter than 6,980 kg/m³, floats on heavier ones
- **Falls:** up to 160 cells/s
- **Freezes:** below 1,538 °C, into iron
- **Conducts:** current with almost no resistance

- **Water:** Molten iron sinks through water (6,980 vs 1,000 kg/m³). Molten iron (1,600 °C) is hot enough to boil water into steam.

### Meat

Raw red meat. Stays put. Warm it and it cooks; left in water it slowly rots.

- **State:** Solid, 1,050 kg/m³
- **Bakes:** at 70 °C into cooked meat; there is no way back
- **Rots:** slowly into dirt where water touches it
- **Hardness:** 0.2 (acid stronger than this eats it)

With other elements (2 interact):

- **Water:** Meat slowly rots into dirt where water touches it.
- **Acid:** Acid eats meat: acidity 0.8 beats hardness 0.2.

### Cooked meat

Browned, cooked meat. Stays put. Overdone it chars into charcoal, and in open air it burns.

- **Rots:** slowly into dirt where water touches it

### Hydrogen peroxide

A pale blue liquid that carries spare oxygen. Flows and sinks through water. It feeds fire, and breaks down into water and oxygen when heated or on rust.

- **State:** Liquid, 1,450 kg/m³
- **In liquids:** Sinks through liquids lighter than 1,450 kg/m³, floats on heavier ones
- **Falls:** up to 160 cells/s
- **Bakes:** at 150 °C into water, giving off oxygen; there is no way back
- **Feeds fire:** strength 0.8 (air is 0.21)

### Saltpeter

White crystals that carry oxygen, a powder. Falls and piles, and dissolves in water. Fuel touching it burns fiercely.

- **State:** Powder, 2,100 kg/m³
- **In liquids:** Sinks through liquids lighter than 2,100 kg/m³, rests on heavier ones
- **Falls:** up to 160 cells/s
- **Feeds fire:** strength 0.9 (air is 0.21)
- **Dissolves in:** water, up to 30% of a cell; boiling leaves it as crystals

### Uranium

A dense, radioactive metal. Stays put and keeps itself warm from its own decay, and poisons living things it touches. Packed together in a big enough pile it goes critical: a chain reaction heats it until it melts down, and can blow it apart.

- **State:** Solid, 19,050 kg/m³
- **Melts:** at 1,132 °C, into corium
- **Conducts:** current with almost no resistance
- **Chain reaction:** about 45 fuel cells within 5 cells make it critical: it heats, melts down and can blow apart
- **Poisons:** living things it touches: they wither
- **Hardness:** 0.6 (acid stronger than this eats it)

### Bromine vapour

A choking red-brown vapour, very heavy. Sinks and pools low, kills plants, and condenses back into bromine as it cools.

- **Condenses:** below 59 °C, into bromine

### Plague

A drifting green mist of germs. Sinks slowly and fades. Any animal it touches falls sick: it runs a fever, passes the sickness to animals it touches, and dies of it unless medicine reaches it. Heat kills the germs.

- **State:** Gas, 1.3 kg/m³
- **In air:** Sinks slowly (heavier than air)
- **Infects:** animals it touches: fever, spreading, death unless cured
- **Bakes:** at 80 °C into air; there is no way back

### Corium

Molten nuclear fuel from a meltdown, white-hot and very heavy. Oozes slowly and sinks through almost everything. It keeps heating itself while enough of it is together, and sets back into uranium only if it cools.

- **State:** Liquid, 17,000 kg/m³
- **Starts at:** 1,400 °C
- **In liquids:** Sinks through liquids lighter than 17,000 kg/m³, floats on heavier ones
- **Freezes:** below 1,132 °C, into uranium
- **Chain reaction:** about 45 fuel cells within 5 cells make it critical: it heats, melts down and can blow apart
- **Poisons:** living things it touches: they wither

With other elements (155 interact):

- **Water:** Corium sinks through water (17,000 vs 1,000 kg/m³). Corium (1,400 °C) is hot enough to boil water into steam.
- **Oil:** Corium sinks through oil (17,000 vs 900 kg/m³). Corium (1,400 °C) can set oil on fire (it ignites at 250 °C).
- **Ice:** Corium (1,400 °C) is hot enough to melt ice into water. Ice (-20 °C) is cold enough to freeze corium into uranium.
- **Steam:** Corium falls through steam.
- **Lava:** Corium sinks through lava (17,000 vs 2,600 kg/m³).
- **Stone:** Corium (1,400 °C) is hot enough to melt stone into lava.
- **Gravel:** Corium (1,400 °C) is hot enough to melt gravel into lava.
- **Fire:** Corium falls through fire.
- **Smoke:** Corium falls through smoke.
- **Wood:** Corium (1,400 °C) can set wood on fire (it ignites at 300 °C).
- **Acid:** Corium sinks through acid (17,000 vs 1,100 kg/m³).
- **Hydrogen:** Corium falls through hydrogen. Corium (1,400 °C) can set hydrogen on fire (it ignites at 500 °C).
- **Oxygen:** Corium falls through oxygen.
- **Methane:** Corium falls through methane. Corium (1,400 °C) can set methane on fire (it ignites at 540 °C).
- **Alcohol:** Corium sinks through alcohol (17,000 vs 789 kg/m³). Corium (1,400 °C) can set alcohol on fire (it ignites at 365 °C).
- **Sawdust:** Corium (1,400 °C) can set sawdust on fire (it ignites at 260 °C).

### Control rod

A boron carbide rod that soaks up neutrons. Stays put. Set among uranium, it slows or stops the chain reaction; pull it out and the pile heats up.

- **State:** Solid, 2,520 kg/m³
- **Absorbs:** neutrons, slowing a chain reaction nearby
- **Hardness:** 0.95 (acid stronger than this eats it)

### Dough

Flour mixed with water, a soft sticky lump. Falls and slumps. Baked past 180 °C it rises into bread.

- **State:** Powder, 1,100 kg/m³
- **In liquids:** Sinks through liquids lighter than 1,100 kg/m³, rests on heavier ones
- **Bakes:** at 180 °C into bread, giving off steam; there is no way back
- **Hardness:** 0.2 (acid stronger than this eats it)

### Epoxy

Set two-part epoxy, a tough clear amber solid. Stays put and reaches far past its support. It burns only in strong heat.

- **State:** Solid, 1,200 kg/m³
- **Burns:** from 450 °C in air, 3.33 s per cell, leaves ash
- **Span:** reaches 14 cells past its support; beyond that, or with nothing under it, it breaks off and falls

### Moss

### Fire ice

Methane hydrate: ice with natural gas locked inside. Stays put and very cold. Warmed past 5 °C it falls apart into water and methane, and a flame sets the lump burning like ice on fire.

- **State:** Solid, 900 kg/m³
- **Starts at:** -20 °C
- **Burns:** from 120 °C in air, 2 s per cell, leaves water
- **Span:** reaches 4 cells past its support; beyond that, or with nothing under it, it breaks off and falls
- **Bakes:** at 5 °C into water, giving off methane; there is no way back
- **Hardness:** 0.3 (acid stronger than this eats it)

### Solar panel

A photovoltaic cell. Stays put and works like a battery that never runs flat, but its voltage follows the light on it: full in open daylight, weak in shade, nothing in the dark. A longer panel gives more volts.

- **State:** Solid, 2,400 kg/m³
- **Powers:** 0.6 V for each cell along the wire, round a closed loop; turns itself round to help other batteries; runs flat with use
- **Powers:** 0.6 V a cell in full daylight, less in shade
- **Hardness:** 0.7 (acid stronger than this eats it)

With other elements (1 interact):

- **Acid:** Acid eats solar panel: acidity 0.8 beats hardness 0.7.

### Steel beam

A rolled steel girder. Stays put and holds itself out a very long way from its support, so it can bridge wide gaps that stone or brick never could. Great heat softens it into molten iron.

- **State:** Solid, 7,850 kg/m³
- **Conducts:** current with almost no resistance
- **Span:** reaches 60 cells past its support; beyond that, or with nothing under it, it breaks off and falls
- **Bakes:** at 1,500 °C into molten iron; there is no way back
- **Hardness:** 0.95 (acid stronger than this eats it)

### Rope

Twisted hemp rope. Hangs from whatever it is tied to and holds up what hangs below it, but it pushes nothing up and holds nothing sideways. It burns, and whatever it held falls.

- **State:** Solid, 600 kg/m³
- **Burns:** from 250 °C in air, 1.5 s per cell, leaves ash
- **Hangs:** holds up what hangs below it, but nothing sideways
- **Hardness:** 0.3 (acid stronger than this eats it)

With other elements (26 interact):

- **Air:** Rope burns: it catches fire at 250 °C next to air (oxidiser 0.21).
- **Lava:** Lava (1,200 °C) can set rope on fire (it ignites at 250 °C).
- **Fire:** Rope catches from the flame touching it.
- **Acid:** Acid eats rope: acidity 0.8 beats hardness 0.3.

### Valve

A pressure relief valve. Stays put and seals like a wall until the air pressure on it climbs past its setting; then it opens (bright) and lets gas through, closing again as the pressure falls.

- **State:** Solid, 7,800 kg/m³

### Ammonium nitrate

White fertiliser crystals, a powder. Dissolving in water, it makes the water ice cold, as in a cold pack. It feeds fire, and great heat makes it explode.

- **State:** Powder, 1,720 kg/m³
- **In liquids:** Sinks through liquids lighter than 1,720 kg/m³, rests on heavier ones
- **Falls:** up to 160 cells/s
- **Explodes:** from 400 °C or a flame; blast radius 5 cells
- **A flame:** will not light it; it needs 400 °C or a spark
- **Dissolving:** makes the water colder (a cold pack)
- **Feeds fire:** strength 0.6 (air is 0.21)
- **Dissolves in:** water, up to 60% of a cell; boiling leaves it as crystals
